gap: Lighting and atmospheric depth (image A). With the same camera, (1) one directional sun must make every building cast a crisp shadow onto the streets and neighbouring roofs (no building without a visible cast shadow), and (2) the far downtown towers across the bay must sit in sun-tinted haze: their facades clearly lower in contrast and shifted toward the sky colour, roughly half the near-block contrast or less, so three depth layers (near / mid / far) are easy to tell apart.

- No render refusals or queue waits: the GPU slot was acquired immediately each time. No references were blocked.. Judge: The commercial game wins all four pairs clearly, and none of them is close. In every frame the in-development game reads as a prototype. Lighting is mostly ambient with weak or missing sun shadows, except pair 4, where a warm low sun casts believable long shadows. Distant skylines have almost no haze to show distance, so near and far buildings have the same contrast. Buildings are low-poly boxes with tiled window textures, and landmark pieces like the Ferris wheel and tree towers are recognisable but crude. The bay water is a matte grey plane with no reflections. Roads carry almost no traffic and there are almost no people, and large flat ground areas are left empty. The HUD is placeholder (an empty grid minimap with a visible mouse pointer). The commercial frames win on three things the in-development game does not try yet: depth from sunlit haze, life in every layer (traffic, aircraft, people), and deliberate composition (foreground framing, dutch angles, dusk or backlight). The most valuable fixes, in order: a directional sun with shadows plus distance haze; enough traffic and pedestrians to fill the roads; material detail on roads and ground; water that reflects sky and skyline; and more varied building facades. Pair 4 shows the ground-level renderer is getting close on light; what is missing there is mainly life and surface detail.
